noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: describe ultrafiltration in the Bowman’s capsule and the composition of the glomerular filtrate
understand how water is reabsorbed into the blood from the collecting duct
understand why selective reabsorption of glucose occurs at the proximal convoluted tubule

primer.text: Urine does not simply appear — it is built in three stages along the nephron. You already know the kidney filters blood; this note walks the filtrate from the glomerulus, through the glucose rescue at the proximal convoluted tubule, to the water tuning at the collecting duct you met in the ADH note.

lessons.title: Ultrafiltration
lessons.opening: The first stage happens in the glomerulus, the knot of capillaries tucked inside each Bowman's capsule. Blood arrives under high pressure — the vessel feeding in is wider than the one leaving, so pressure piles up — and that pressure shoves small molecules through a sieve-like membrane into the capsule. Water, glucose, urea and ions cross; proteins and blood cells are too bulky and stay behind.
keyPoints: Three stages build urine: ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption and water reabsorption.
Ultrafiltration happens in the glomerulus under unusually high blood pressure.
The vessel entering the glomerulus is wider than the vessel leaving it, which forces the pressure up.
The sieve-like membrane passes small molecules and holds back proteins and cells.
The fluid caught in the Bowman's capsule is the glomerular filtrate.

low.restatement: High pressure squeezes the small molecules of the blood into the Bowman's capsule.
low.analogy: It is a coffee press: hot water forced through a mesh leaves the grounds behind.
low.examPointer: Always list the filtrate's contents — water, glucose, urea, ions — and name what stays behind.

medium.restatement: Describe the sieving as squeezing under pressure; large molecules never leave the blood at all.
medium.analogy: A sieve under a tap: fine grains wash through, pebbles stay in the mesh.
medium.examPointer: Say forced out by pressure rather than diffused — mark schemes penalise the diffusion slip.

check.stem: Where does ultrafiltration take place?

options.text: In the glomerulus inside the Bowman's capsule
options.explanation: That is the filtration site named in the specification.
The collecting duct handles water reabsorption, the final stage.
The loop concentrates the filtrate; it does not filter blood.
The ureter only carries urine towards the bladder.

check.stem: Which substances are present in the glomerular filtrate?

options.explanation: These four cross the filter; everything larger stays in the blood.
Protein never crosses the filtration membrane.

options.text: Water, glucose and red blood cells
options.explanation: Blood cells are far too large to filter through.
Water and ions cross too; the list is not that short.

check.stem: Why is blood pressure especially high inside the glomerulus?

options.text: The vessel entering is wider than the vessel leaving, so pressure builds
options.explanation: That width difference forces the pressure up at the filtration site.

options.text: The heart pumps extra hard towards the kidneys
options.explanation: No extra pumping occurs; geometry does the work.
The capsule surrounds but does not squeeze.

options.text: Because the blood is thicker there
options.explanation: Blood thickness does not change at the glomerulus.

check.stem: What stops proteins from entering the filtrate?

options.text: They are too large to pass the filtration membrane
options.explanation: Size alone excludes them at the sieve.
Nothing transports proteins back; they never leave the blood.

options.text: They dissolve out of the filtrate
options.explanation: They simply never cross in the first place.
Nothing destroys proteins at the capsule.

check.stem: Which process description matches ultrafiltration?

options.text: Small molecules are forced out of the blood under pressure
options.explanation: Forcing under pressure is the defining feature of this stage.

options.text: Glucose is pulled back into the blood by active transport
options.explanation: That is selective reabsorption, the second stage.

options.text: Water leaves the collecting duct by osmosis
options.explanation: That is water reabsorption, the third stage.

options.text: Urea diffuses slowly out of the blood
options.explanation: Urea is forced out with the rest of the filtrate, not diffused.

check.stem: Name the fluid that collects in the Bowman's capsule.
List the three processes that turn filtrate into urine, in order.
check.modelAnswer: Ultrafiltration, then selective reabsorption of glucose, then reabsorption of water.

check.stem: Explain why ultrafiltration is described as a pressure-driven process rather than diffusion.
check.modelAnswer: Because the high pressure built up in the glomerulus physically forces small molecules through the sieve-like membrane; no concentration gradient is doing the work, which is what diffusion would require.

check.stem: A student says 'the glomerulus filters urea out because the blood does not want it'. Sharpen this into the examinable mechanism.
check.modelAnswer: Better: the glomerulus is a high-pressure filtration point — the width difference between the vessels entering and leaving builds pressure that forces small molecules, including urea, through the membrane into the Bowman's capsule; the sieving is mechanical, so selectivity is by size, not by usefulness.

lessons.title: Selective Reabsorption of Glucose
lessons.opening: The filtrate still carries glucose the body intends to keep. All of it is reclaimed in the proximal convoluted tubule by active transport, which pushes glucose against its gradient into the surrounding capillaries. That push costs energy, which is why the PCT's cells are packed with mitochondria.
keyPoints: All the glucose in the filtrate is reabsorbed at the proximal convoluted tubule.
Glucose moves against its concentration gradient, so active transport is required.
Active transport needs energy, supplied by the PCT cells' many mitochondria.
Urea stays in the filtrate because it is waste, not because it cannot be moved.
The word selective means useful substances are rescued and wastes are left.

low.restatement: The PCT wins back every trace of glucose before the fluid goes further.
low.analogy: A security checkpoint that waves every familiar face through and lets the strangers pass.
low.examPointer: Name active transport and mitochondria together — the energy story earns the marks.

medium.restatement: Glucose is fully rescued in the PCT by energy-costing transport.
medium.analogy: Like paying a porter to carry every dropped coin back up the hill, against the flow.
medium.examPointer: Pair the words active transport and mitochondria; one without the other loses the mark.

check.stem: Where is glucose reabsorbed from the filtrate?

options.explanation: The PCT is the reabsorption site for glucose.
The glomerulus filters; reabsorption happens further along.
The collecting duct handles water, not glucose.
The loop's job is concentration, not glucose rescue.

check.stem: Why does glucose reabsorption need active transport?

options.text: Glucose moves against its concentration gradient
options.explanation: Uphill movement demands energy; passive processes only go downhill.

options.text: Because glucose molecules are very large
options.explanation: Size is not the issue; the gradient direction is.

options.text: Because the tubule walls are thick
options.explanation: Wall thickness plays no role in the gradient story.

options.text: Because glucose dissolves poorly in water
options.explanation: Glucose dissolves readily; that is not the constraint.

check.stem: What provides the energy for glucose reabsorption?

options.explanation: The many mitochondria supply the ATP the active transport needs.
Pressure drives ultrafiltration, not active transport.
Cilia belong to the airways, not the nephron.
ADH directs water reabsorption in the collecting duct.

check.stem: How much glucose does a healthy person lose in urine?

options.text: None — all of it is reabsorbed
options.explanation: The reabsorption at the PCT is total.
A healthy nephron loses nothing; a trickle signals a problem.
There is no such threshold in this model — reabsorption is complete.
Half would waste the body's fuel; the design reclaims all.

check.stem: Which statement about urea in the filtrate is correct?

options.text: It stays in the filtrate and becomes more concentrated as water leaves
options.explanation: Urea is waste; it rides the fluid onwards and concentrates.

options.text: It is actively reabsorbed like glucose
options.explanation: Active reabsorption is reserved for useful substances.

options.text: It is broken down inside the tubule
options.explanation: Nothing breaks urea down in the nephron.

options.text: It never enters the filtrate at all
options.explanation: Urea is small enough to filter and does enter the filtrate.

check.stem: Name the tubule where glucose is selectively reabsorbed.
Which two features of the PCT suit it to active transport?
check.modelAnswer: Its cells carry many mitochondria, and active transport moves glucose against its gradient.

check.stem: Explain why the term selective is used for this reabsorption.
check.modelAnswer: Because the process rescues the useful substance — glucose — while leaving wastes such as urea in the filtrate; the tubule distinguishes between what the body keeps and what it discards, which is exactly what selective means here.

check.stem: A rare disorder leaves PCT mitochondria scarce. Predict the urine and explain.
check.modelAnswer: With too few mitochondria the active transport of glucose loses power, so glucose would remain in the filtrate and appear in the urine — the same signature seen when blood glucose runs far above normal, because the rescue machinery cannot cope.

lessons.title: Reabsorption of Water
lessons.opening: The last stage hands control back to the hormone you met earlier. Filtrate leaving the PCT passes the loop of Henle and the distal convoluted tubule before reaching the collecting duct, where the majority of the remaining water returns to the blood by osmosis. How much returns depends on ADH: more hormone, more water reclaimed, and a concentrated urine; less hormone, and the water departs in a dilute stream.
keyPoints: After the PCT, filtrate flows through the loop of Henle, the DCT and the collecting duct.
Some water leaves in the loop of Henle, but most is reclaimed at the collecting duct.
Water crosses the collecting duct by osmosis into the blood.
ADH sets how permeable the duct is, and therefore how much water is reclaimed.
More ADH concentrates the urine; less ADH dilutes it.

low.restatement: Water leaves the collecting duct by osmosis, and ADH decides how much.
low.analogy: A clothes line in changing weather: the drier the air, the more water the laundry gives up.
low.examPointer: Tie the hormone to the outcome — ADH up, concentrated urine — in one sentence.

medium.restatement: The collecting duct is the adjustable water gate; ADH holds the handle.
medium.analogy: A dam with movable sluice gates: how far they open decides the river's flow.
medium.examPointer: Answer water questions with the chain: ADH, permeability, osmosis, urine concentration.

check.stem: From which structure is most water reabsorbed into the blood?

options.explanation: Most of the reabsorption happens there, under ADH's control.
The glomerulus filters blood; it does not reabsorb water.
The capsule catches the filtrate; nothing is reabsorbed there.
Some water leaves in the loop, but the majority crosses the duct.

check.stem: By which process does water leave the collecting duct?

options.explanation: Water moves down its potential gradient through the duct wall.
Active transport is the glucose story; water needs no pumping.
That is the pressure-driven first stage, in reverse territory here.
Nothing evaporates inside the kidney.

check.stem: What happens to the urine when ADH release rises?

options.text: It becomes smaller in volume and more concentrated
options.explanation: More reclaimed water means less, stronger urine.
That is the low-ADH outcome.
ADH acts precisely on the duct's water permeability.
Waste still leaves; the volume only shrinks.

check.stem: Which structures does the filtrate pass through after the PCT?

options.text: The loop of Henle, the distal convoluted tubule, then the collecting duct
options.explanation: That is the downstream sequence of the nephron.

options.text: The glomerulus, then the Bowman's capsule
options.explanation: Those are the upstream filtration structures.

options.text: The ureter, then the bladder directly
options.explanation: Those come after the nephron has finished its work.

options.text: The loop of Henle, then the glomerulus
options.explanation: Fluid never returns to the glomerulus.

check.stem: Why is the collecting duct called the site of osmoregulation?

options.text: Because adjusting water reabsorption there is how the blood's water content is controlled
options.explanation: The duct's variable permeability is the body's water lever.

options.text: Because it stores urine between passes
options.explanation: Storage is the bladder's job.

options.text: Because it filters proteins from the blood
options.explanation: Protein handling belongs to the glomerulus's membrane.
The pituitary makes ADH; the duct merely responds.

check.stem: Name the hormone that controls water reabsorption at the collecting duct.
check.modelAnswer: ADH, the antidiuretic hormone from the pituitary gland.

check.stem: Through which three structures does filtrate pass after the PCT?
check.modelAnswer: The loop of Henle, the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct.

check.stem: Explain why water leaves the collecting duct by osmosis rather than by active transport.
check.modelAnswer: Because water simply moves down its potential gradient from the dilute filtrate towards the more concentrated blood whenever the duct wall allows it; no energy is spent, and the wall's permeability — set by ADH — is all the control the body needs.

check.stem: A diuretic drink suppresses ADH for an afternoon. Trace the effect through the collecting duct to the urine.
check.modelAnswer: With ADH lowered the duct walls stay tight against water, so little is reclaimed by osmosis; a large volume of pale, dilute urine carries the water away, which is exactly the response to surplus blood water.

glossary.definition: Pressure-driven filtering of small blood molecules into the Bowman's capsule at the glomerulus.
The fluid caught in the Bowman's capsule: water, glucose, urea and ions, minus proteins and cells.
The reclamation of useful substances, chiefly all the glucose, at the proximal convoluted tubule.
The movement of water across a membrane towards the more concentrated solution.
